transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I’m here because things kind of blew up at work. I work in HR, and there was this onboarding launch we’d been talking about forever, and I just… pushed it ahead. I committed company money and vendor time before all the approvals were actually in place.

At the time it felt like the right move, like bold and necessary, you know? Like if I didn’t drive it forward, it would just die in meetings like everything else. But now I’m on leave, and people keep asking me what I was thinking, and honestly I’m not sure how to answer that without sounding ridiculous.
During the time you pushed the project ahead, were you needing much less sleep than usual?

I don’t know, honestly. I mean, that whole stretch is kind of blurry because the launch was taking over everything, and I’d be up thinking about vendor timelines or whether Legal was going to drag their feet again, and then I’d remember some completely unrelated thing, like this one compliance training rollout from years ago where everyone blamed HR for delays even though it wasn’t really us.

So… I’m not sure I’d say I needed less sleep exactly. I just wasn’t paying close attention to it.
During that time, did you feel unusually high, euphoric, or especially irritable?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, not “happy” exactly, not like vacation happy. More like I felt brilliantly alive, like I could finally show leadership what HR is supposed to be, not just paperwork and policy reminders.

And then if someone questioned me — even something small, like an edit to a deck or a routine budget question — I’d get furious. Like, disproportionate furious. Which is strange because normally I can sit through endless feedback meetings, that’s basically half of HR, but during those weeks it felt like everyone was trying to slow me down or make me smaller.
During that period, did you feel driven to take on a lot more projects or activities than usual?

Yeah, definitely. I mean… it didn’t feel like “a lot” at the time, it felt like finally doing what should have been done already.

I was trying to run the HR redesign, and at the same time I was reaching out to gallery partners — which, I know, sounds unrelated, but there was this idea about making the onboarding experience more connected to local culture, and then that made me think of festivals, so I started contacting festival organizers too. And then there were these staff conflicts that had been sitting around forever, so I was jumping into those like, “I can fix this today.”

It was like every idea had to be acted on immediately, before anyone could bury it in another committee meeting.
During that period, did you feel unusually powerful or especially certain that your ideas were uniquely important?

I’m… not totally sure how to answer that. “Powerful” sounds a little dramatic, doesn’t it? I mean, I was confident, maybe very confident, but at work you’re sort of expected to sell the vision. If you don’t sound convinced, then everyone piles on with doubts and suddenly you’re in a meeting about a meeting.

The “uniquely important” part… I don’t know. I remember feeling like people weren’t seeing the obvious path, but that happens in HR more than people realize. Everyone thinks HR is just forms and complaints, but there’s strategy there, culture, retention, all of it. Like when we changed the performance review templates years ago, everyone acted like it was just a document, but it changed the whole tone of manager conversations.

So… maybe I felt strongly that my ideas mattered, but I don’t know if I’d call it unusually powerful. I’d have to think about that.
During that time, were you sleeping much less than usual and still feeling full of energy the next day?

I’m not sure, honestly. Sleep is one of those things I only notice after the fact, if that makes sense. I don’t keep track of it very well.

I mean, I’ve had busy stretches where I’m up late thinking about work or answering one more email, but I don’t know that I could say, “Yes, I was sleeping much less and felt great the next day.” I’d have to think about it more. My wife would probably have a better read on that than I do — she notices things like whether I’m getting up at weird hours or moving around the house.

So… I’m not saying no exactly, I just don’t have a clear answer.
During that time, did you believe things that other people said were not true or unrealistic?

I don’t know. I mean, “not true” is a hard thing, because in an office people call things unrealistic all the time when what they really mean is inconvenient or not in the budget yet.

Like, I’d suggest something and people would say, “That’s not how we do things,” but that’s not the same as it being false, right? HR is full of that — policies that everyone treats like laws of nature, and then six months later leadership changes and suddenly the impossible thing is mandatory.

So… I don’t think I believed anything obviously untrue. At least not that I remember. But if you mean did other people think I was being unrealistic about my plans, maybe, yes, they probably did. I’m not sure that’s the same thing though.
Before this recent period at work, have you ever had another time in your life when you felt unusually energized or driven in a similar way?

Yeah… I mean, I’m trying to think before the work situation, and I don’t know if I’d call it the same, exactly. But there have definitely been stretches where I get this… drive, like I can’t just sit and wait for things to happen.

Like I’ll get in early, before most people are even settled, and I’m already walking the floors, checking in on what teams are doing, looking at conference rooms like I’m mapping a campaign or something. Then I’m back rewriting decks that were probably fine the night before, sending emails to people because some piece of the plan suddenly seems obvious, rearranging timelines, moving things around.

It’s not even always that I feel stressed. It’s more like my body has a motor in it. Sitting at my desk feels almost impossible, like I should be up fixing something or connecting dots. Which… in HR, that can look productive, honestly. People like when you’re proactive. But yes, I guess there have been times like that.
Between these driven periods, do you return to your usual self?

I’m not totally sure how to measure “usual self,” I guess. I mean, day to day I still go to work, still do the grocery run, still answer emails — although email is a terrible measure because nobody is ever really caught up, you know?

My wife might say there are times I’m more settled, maybe less… I don’t know, keyed into everything. But from the inside it’s hard to tell. You just sort of keep moving, and then later someone says, “You were different that month,” and I’m thinking, was I? Or was that just a busy quarter?

So I don’t have a clean yes-or-no answer. I think there are stretches where things feel more normal, but I don’t always notice the transition.
During those driven periods, do you find yourself talking much more than usual?

Yeah… I think so. I don’t always notice it in the moment, because in a meeting you’re supposed to be talking, right? Especially HR — half the job is explaining things everyone already half-understands but in a way that doesn’t make anyone panic.

But there are times I can hear myself going faster, like I’ve started on employee engagement, and then suddenly I’m talking about gallery layouts — because the office space affects morale, which affects retention, so it connects — and then I’m on retention metrics and survey design and who needs to be looped in. And I’m still talking.

People kind of sit there waiting for a gap, and sometimes they practically have to raise their hands to get me to stop or ask a question. So… yes, during those periods I probably talk more than usual.
During these periods, do you become much more active than usual, like constantly starting tasks or moving from one project to another?

Yes. That’s probably one of the clearer things, actually.

I’ll start one thing and then it’s like another piece lights up, and I’m already moving to that. Like I’ve been trying to run this HR redesign, but then also lining up gallery partners, and then I’ll think, oh, we should contact the festival organizers now, not next week, and then there are three staff conflicts that I suddenly feel like I have to fix immediately.

It’s not like I calmly make a list and work through it. It’s more like every idea feels time-sensitive, like if I don’t act on it right then, the whole thing loses momentum. And then I’m bouncing between all of it.
During one of these driven periods, have you ever been hospitalized because of your behavior?

Hospitalized? No, I don’t think so. I mean, not in the sense of being admitted or kept somewhere because of how I was acting.

There was one time my wife said I should “talk to someone before this turns into a thing,” but that’s not the same as a hospital. And honestly, hospitals make me think of my dad’s knee surgery, that whole fluorescent-light waiting room feeling, vending machine coffee… sorry, that’s not what you asked.

So, no, I haven’t been hospitalized for it.
During those energized periods, do you feel more important or more capable than other people?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. “More important” sounds… I don’t know, like I’m walking around thinking I’m royalty or something, and I don’t think that’s me.

More capable, maybe I feel like I can see the whole board at once, if that makes sense. But then again, in HR you kind of have to act like you know what you’re doing even when everyone’s looking at you to explain a policy that was written by someone in legal ten years ago. I remember this one benefits meeting where the projector wouldn’t connect, and somehow I ended up troubleshooting cables while also talking through open enrollment, and people were joking that I should run IT too—

Sorry, I’m wandering. I don’t really know. I guess I haven’t noticed myself thinking I’m better than other people, exactly. More like I feel… very sure I can handle things.
During one of these energized periods, have other people clearly told you that you were acting unlike yourself?

Yeah… a couple people have said something like that. My wife especially. She’ll say, “You’re not yourself right now,” usually after I’ve gotten really intense about something that probably didn’t need to be that intense.

At work too, not always directly, but I can tell. Like for the past few weeks I’ve felt… I don’t know, brilliantly alive sometimes, like I can finally show leadership what HR is supposed to be, not just forms and compliance and awkward trainings in a conference room with stale muffins. And then if someone questions me — even a small edit, or a routine budget question — I can just snap into being furious, like they’re trying to sabotage the whole thing.

So yes, people have made it clear I’m acting different. I don’t always agree in the moment, but later I can see why they said it.
Have you ever had one of these energized periods that lasted at least a full week?

Yeah… definitely at least a week. This current one has been going on longer than that, honestly.

It’s been building for about a month now, since the new executive started pushing back on my onboarding redesign. Which sounds so boring when I say it out loud — onboarding, forms, welcome emails, who gets a badge on day one — but it’s not just that. It’s like she questioned one piece of it, and then suddenly the whole thing became this… I don’t know, campaign in my head.

Sorry, yes — to answer your actual question, yes. More than a week. About a month.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

I don’t know if I can say “nearly every day” in that exact way. I’ve had stretches where I felt really low, sure, but two full weeks where it was most of the day every day… I’m not sure.

Part of me wants to say yes because everyone gets ground down eventually, especially when work is just this constant stream of people’s problems—complaints, benefits issues, someone crying in my office because their manager is awful—and you carry that home even when you pretend you don’t. But that’s not the same thing as what you’re asking, probably.

So… I don’t know. I can’t clearly point to a two-week period like that.
Have you ever had a time when you felt depressed nearly every day for two weeks or longer?

I’m still not sure I can give you a clean yes on that. I mean, I’ve had bad stretches, I’ve definitely had days where I felt heavy or worn down, but when you say nearly every day for two weeks or longer… I can’t really point to that and say, yes, that happened.

It gets blurry, you know? Work weeks can all run together, and then suddenly it’s Friday and I’m thinking about some benefits audit or whether I forgot to respond to someone’s leave paperwork, and I’ll feel awful, but I don’t know if that’s the same as what you mean.

So… I don’t know. I don’t think I can say yes to that.
Have you ever had a period when you lost interest or pleasure in almost everything you usually enjoy?

I’m not sure. I don’t think so in some total way, like everything went flat. I’ve had times where I didn’t feel like doing much, but then I’ll still get pulled into something—some article, or fixing something in the apartment, or honestly even reorganizing a spreadsheet because it’s bothering me.

It’s hard because “interest” is weird. Sometimes I don’t want to see people, but that might be because I’m tired of people after dealing with employees all day. HR is basically being everyone’s emotional baggage claim, and then people act like you should still want to go to dinner afterward and make small talk about vacation plans.

So… I don’t know. I can’t really say I’ve lost interest or pleasure in almost everything. Not that I can clearly remember.
Have you ever had a time when, for two weeks or longer, you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

I know you’ve asked it a couple times, and I’m not trying to dodge it. I just… I really don’t have a clear memory of a solid two-week stretch like that, where I was depressed most of the day nearly every day.

There have been times I felt lousy, absolutely. Sometimes work just drains the color out of everything for a while, especially when you’re listening to people complain or panic or accuse HR of being the enemy all day. Then I go home and I’m still replaying conversations in my head, like, “Did I say that wrong?” or “Is this going to become a whole issue?”

But if you’re asking specifically about two weeks or more, most of the day, nearly every day… I can’t honestly say yes. I’m not sure.
Before this current month, have you ever had another period lasting at least a week when you felt unusually energized or driven like this?

Yeah—well, I mean, at least something like that has happened before. I don’t always notice it as “energized” at first. It feels more like I’m suddenly moving faster than the room is built for.

I’ll get to work early, like earlier than I need to, and start walking the floors instead of just going to my desk. Then I’m rewriting decks that were already fine, sending emails to people because I’ve thought of a better way to do something, rearranging plans, moving pieces around. It’s like my body has a motor in it.

And sitting at my desk during that kind of stretch feels almost impossible. I’ll tell myself, “Just sit down and finish one thing,” but then I’m up again, checking on something or changing something. It can go on for days. I’m not great at pinning down whether it was exactly a week every time, but yes, before this month I’ve had periods like that.

I remember this one benefits meeting where the projector wouldn’t connect, and somehow I ended up troubleshooting cables while also talking through open enrollment, and people were joking that I should run IT too—

Sorry, I’m wandering. I don’t really know. I guess I haven’t noticed myself thinking I’m better than other people, exactly. More like I feel… very sure I can handle things.

doctor.intent: Determine whether these energized periods cause clear functional impairment recognizable to others, which helps distinguish a hypomanic/manic syndrome from personality-based or stress-related patterns.
doctor.question: During one of these energized periods, have other people clearly told you that you were acting unlike yourself?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: For the past few weeks I've felt either brilliantly alive, like I could finally show leadership what HR can be, or suddenly furious when someone questioned me, even over small edits or routine budget questions.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether others noticed a clear change in behavior during the energized periods, which most directly relates to an abnormally elevated or irritable mood state being apparent to others.

patient.answer:
Yeah… a couple people have said something like that. My wife especially. She’ll say, “You’re not yourself right now,” usually after I’ve gotten really intense about something that probably didn’t need to be that intense.

At work too, not always directly, but I can tell. Like for the past few weeks I’ve felt… I don’t know, brilliantly alive sometimes, like I can finally show leadership what HR is supposed to be, not just forms and compliance and awkward trainings in a conference room with stale muffins. And then if someone questions me — even a small edit, or a routine budget question — I can just snap into being furious, like they’re trying to sabotage the whole thing.

So yes, people have made it clear I’m acting different. I don’t always agree in the moment, but later I can see why they said it.

inference.note: Repeated periods of elevated/irritable mood, increased talkativeness, marked increase in goal-directed activity, risky/impulsive work decisions, and others noticing clear change from baseline support a bipolar spectrum manic/hypomanic syndrome. Personality/stress-related candidates are less supported; no clear psychosis or hospitalization yet, so keep F31.1 and F30.1 pending clarification of prior depressive episodes and episode duration/severity.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a full manic episode lasting at least one week, which would distinguish bipolar I disorder from a single current manic episode diagnosis.
doctor.question: Have you ever had one of these energized periods that lasted at least a full week?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been building for about a month, since the new executive started challenging my onboarding redesign.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the energized periods last, specifically whether they lasted at least a full week.

patient.answer:
Yeah… definitely at least a week. This current one has been going on longer than that, honestly.

It’s been building for about a month now, since the new executive started pushing back on my onboarding redesign. Which sounds so boring when I say it out loud — onboarding, forms, welcome emails, who gets a badge on day one — but it’s not just that. It’s like she questioned one piece of it, and then suddenly the whole thing became this… I don’t know, campaign in my head.

Sorry, yes — to answer your actual question, yes. More than a week. About a month.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have ever been major depressive episodes, which would distinguish bipolar I disorder from a manic episode diagnosis.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a depressive episode lasting at least two weeks, but the provided symptom profile only covers manic symptoms, impairment, and duration of the current energized period.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I can say “nearly every day” in that exact way. I’ve had stretches where I felt really low, sure, but two full weeks where it was most of the day every day… I’m not sure.

Part of me wants to say yes because everyone gets ground down eventually, especially when work is just this constant stream of people’s problems—complaints, benefits issues, someone crying in my office because their manager is awful—and you carry that home even when you pretend you don’t. But that’s not the same thing as what you’re asking, probably.

So… I don’t know. I can’t clearly point to a two-week period like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a major depressive episode, which would distinguish bipolar I disorder from a manic episode without bipolar history.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a time when you felt depressed nearly every day for two weeks or longer?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a depressive episode lasting nearly every day for at least two weeks, but the provided symptom profile does not include depressive symptoms or a major depressive episode item.

patient.answer:
I’m still not sure I can give you a clean yes on that. I mean, I’ve had bad stretches, I’ve definitely had days where I felt heavy or worn down, but when you say nearly every day for two weeks or longer… I can’t really point to that and say, yes, that happened.

It gets blurry, you know? Work weeks can all run together, and then suddenly it’s Friday and I’m thinking about some benefits audit or whether I forgot to respond to someone’s leave paperwork, and I’ll feel awful, but I don’t know if that’s the same as what you mean.

So… I don’t know. I don’t think I can say yes to that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a major depressive episode, which would distinguish bipolar I disorder from a manic episode without bipolar diagnosis.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period when you lost interest or pleasure in almost everything you usually enjoy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about loss of interest or pleasure, a depressive/anhedonia symptom, and the provided symptom profile does not include an item covering that.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I don’t think so in some total way, like everything went flat. I’ve had times where I didn’t feel like doing much, but then I’ll still get pulled into something—some article, or fixing something in the apartment, or honestly even reorganizing a spreadsheet because it’s bothering me.

It’s hard because “interest” is weird. Sometimes I don’t want to see people, but that might be because I’m tired of people after dealing with employees all day. HR is basically being everyone’s emotional baggage claim, and then people act like you should still want to go to dinner afterward and make small talk about vacation plans.

So… I don’t know. I can’t really say I’ve lost interest or pleasure in almost everything. Not that I can clearly remember.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a major depressive episode, which would distinguish bipolar I disorder from a single manic episode.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a time when, for two weeks or longer, you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a two-week period of depressed mood nearly every day, but the provided symptom profile only covers manic symptoms, impairment, duration, and risky behavior, not depressive episodes.

patient.answer:
I know you’ve asked it a couple times, and I’m not trying to dodge it. I just… I really don’t have a clear memory of a solid two-week stretch like that, where I was depressed most of the day nearly every day.

There have been times I felt lousy, absolutely. Sometimes work just drains the color out of everything for a while, especially when you’re listening to people complain or panic or accuse HR of being the enemy all day. Then I go home and I’m still replaying conversations in my head, like, “Did I say that wrong?” or “Is this going to become a whole issue?”

But if you’re asking specifically about two weeks or more, most of the day, nearly every day… I can’t honestly say yes. I’m not sure.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had prior manic episodes, which would support bipolar I disorder over a single manic episode.
doctor.question: Before this current month, have you ever had another period lasting at least a week when you felt unusually energized or driven like this?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I keep arriving early, walking the floors, rewriting decks, emailing people, and rearranging plans like my body has a motor in it and sitting at my desk feels almost impossible.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about periods of unusually increased energy or drive, which most directly matches increased activity or energy.

patient.answer:
Yeah—well, I mean, at least something like that has happened before. I don’t always notice it as “energized” at first. It feels more like I’m suddenly moving faster than the room is built for.

I’ll get to work early, like earlier than I need to, and start walking the floors instead of just going to my desk. Then I’m rewriting decks that were already fine, sending emails to people because I’ve thought of a better way to do something, rearranging plans, moving pieces around. It’s like my body has a motor in it.

And sitting at my desk during that kind of stretch feels almost impossible. I’ll tell myself, “Just sit down and finish one thing,” but then I’m up again, checking on something or changing something. It can go on for days. I’m not great at pinning down whether it was exactly a week every time, but yes, before this month I’ve had periods like that.
